narrative.text: Abstract of Doc-Researcher. Deep Research systems are limited to textual web data, while scientific papers, technical reports and financial documents keep critical information in figures, tables, charts and equations. Doc-Researcher combines (i) deep multimodal parsing that keeps layout and visual semantics and builds representations from chunk to document level, (ii) retrieval that supports text-only, vision-only and hybrid paradigms with dynamic granularity selection, and (iii) iterative multi-agent workflows that decompose queries and accumulate evidence. The authors also introduce M4DocBench, a benchmark of 158 expert-annotated questions with complete evidence chains over 304 documents, for multi-modal, multi-hop, multi-document and multi-turn deep research. They report 50.6% accuracy, 3.4× the best baseline. The block ends with the CCS concepts, keywords and the ACM copyright notice.

Introduction. Agentic RAG lets systems plan retrieval, call tools, refine queries and validate context, and it underpins current Deep Research systems; but these work only on textual web data and cannot use a person's own local documents. Multimodal agentic RAG systems such as MDocAgent and M3DocRAG have three limitations, the authors argue: (1) shallow parsing, either OCR text or raw page screenshots, which loses the semantics of charts, tables, figures, equations and layout; (2) retrieval over OCR chunks or whole pages only, with no way to pick a granularity (full text, summary, page or chunk) to suit the query; and (3) single-round visual QA instead of iterative, multi-step research. They add that no evaluation framework tests multimodal document understanding in realistic research settings. The block ends mid-sentence at a page break.

Related work, first two of three directions. Document parsing comes in three kinds: shallow parsing (OCR text only, losing spatial and visual information), deep parsing such as MinerU (layout boxes, equations to LaTeX, tables to structured formats, recently VLM-based), and parsing-free approaches that treat pages as screenshots, which avoids parsing cost but loses fine-grained localisation and copes poorly with dense text. The authors say their framework combines the strengths of the deep and parsing-free kinds. Visual document understanding benchmarks have moved from single pages to multi-page and long documents, but none test multi-document synthesis, multi-turn interaction or evidence-chain annotation, which motivates M4DocBench. The rest of the block is the text layer of Figure 2 (the architecture diagram): labels for the offline parsing and indexing stage and the online research stage.

Despite its heading, this block holds the caption of Figure 2 (the Doc-Researcher architecture: (a) multimodal deep parsing and indexing, (b) multimodal deep research) and the third related-work direction, document RAG. M3DocRAG uses vision-only page retrieval, MDocAgent combines text chunks with screenshots, and VDocRAG adds figure extraction, but all do single-round retrieval at a fixed granularity. The authors present Doc-Researcher as the first deep-research framework for multimodal documents, with dynamic granularity selection and progressive evidence synthesis.

Opening of the method section. Doc-Researcher (Figure 2) has two modules: deep parsing, which turns multimodal documents into structured, multi-granular, searchable units while keeping their multimodal semantics, and deep research, a multi-agent framework that answers complex questions by iterative search and refinement.

Section 3.1, deep multimodal document parsing. Each document is parsed with MinerU into layout elements indexed by document, page and reading order, each with a type (text, table, figure, equation) and a bounding box. Tables and figures are described once by Qwen2.5-VL, as both a coarse summary and a fine-grained description; equations are converted to LaTeX with UniMERNet. This one-time conversion avoids processing multimodal tokens repeatedly. Layout-aware chunking then merges text elements within section boundaries up to a maximum length, keeping page IDs and boxes for citation. Four granularities are built: chunk, page (merged elements or the raw screenshot), full text, and an LLM-written document summary.

Section 3.2, the three retrieval paradigms. Vision-only retrieval encodes raw page screenshots: no parsing cost, but dense vectors represent interleaved text and images poorly, multi-vector retrievers produce thousands of vectors per page (one per 14×14 or 16×16 patch), and the models are large (often over 3B parameters). Text-only retrieval encodes OCR text, chunks and VLM descriptions of visual elements at page or chunk level with small models (often under 1B), at the cost of preprocessing and some lost visual semantics. Hybrid retrieval encodes visual chunks and screenshots directly alongside text, avoiding conversion loss but costing more at inference. Between the paragraphs is the text layer of Table 1, which compares M4DocBench with ten document RAG/VQA datasets on multi-hop, multimodal, multi-document and multi-turn support, question count, annotation type, domains, languages and retrieval annotation; M4DocBench is the only one with all four properties, with 158 questions, 3.8 documents, 7.0 pages and 14.8 layout elements of evidence per question.
Heading-only block: it holds just the number "4.1" of the first subsection of the M4DocBench section, whose text is in the next block.

Section 4.1, why M4DocBench. A deep-research benchmark must test four things: multi-hop reasoning, multimodal integration (at least two modalities per question), multi-document synthesis (each document contributing essential information, with topically similar distractors), and multi-turn dialogue. Table 1 shows that most existing DocVQA/RAG datasets have multi-hop and multimodal evidence but only one has genuine multi-document reasoning; evidence averages under two pages per question; only two give layout-level evidence; and none is multi-turn. A footnote says that adding noise documents to single-document questions does not make a true multi-document setting. M4DocBench is presented as filling these gaps with expert-annotated QA pairs and complete evidence chains.

Section 4.2, domains and documents. Four domains were chosen for multimodal richness, reasoning complexity and practical relevance: research (166 computer-science papers from arXiv and top conferences, averaging 26.7 pages), insurance (43 brochures and policy documents, 11.0 pages), education (56 university programme materials, 7.5 pages) and finance (38 market research reports on A-shares, Hong Kong and NASDAQ, 22.2 pages).

Section 4.3, annotation. PhD- and Master's-level researchers annotated, beyond question-answer pairs, six dimensions: hard-negative documents that are topically similar but lack the needed information; the best retrieval granularity for each query (full text, summary, page or chunk); relevant pages and bounding boxes, following MMDocIR; ground-truth sub-query decompositions; answer-verification checklists for long answers, used for LLM-based judging; and bilingual English and Chinese questions and documents. Figure 1 and Figure 4 show annotation examples.

Section 4.4, benchmark statistics (Table 7). Each of the 158 questions involves 12.7 documents (306.4 pages) on average and up to 42 documents (836 pages), of which 3.8 are relevant. 112 questions need more than one modality; evidence is 40.9% text, 30.2% tables and 28.9% images, and averages 7.0 pages and 14.8 layout elements per question. 58 questions are in multi-turn conversations; questions average 3.9 search clauses, and answers range from 59.7 to 272.0 words.
Heading-only block: it holds just the number "5.1" of the first subsection of the experiments section, whose text is in the next block.

Section 5.1, metrics and benchmarks. Retrieval is scored as recall@k at document, page and layout level: document and page by exact ID match, layout by bounding-box overlap following MMDocIR (parsing-free methods cannot be scored at layout level). The full deep-research workflow is scored on document selection (precision, recall and F1 of the Planner's chosen documents), agentic retrieval (the same recall metrics over the passages accumulated after the search-refine loops), and answer accuracy, judged by an LLM against the annotated checklist; an answer counts as correct only when every checklist item is present. The two benchmarks are M4DocBench and MMDocIR. Most of the block is the text layer of Table 2, recall@10 of text, vision and hybrid retrievers (BM25, E5, BGE-M3, Qwen3-embedding, DSE, ColPali, ColQwen, Jina-embedding-v4 and combinations) on both benchmarks; the block is cut off inside the table.

Section 5.2, setup and baselines. Ten retrievers are tested in three configurations: five text retrievers (BM25, E5, BGE-M3, Qwen3-embedding-0.6B, Qwen3-reranker-0.6B) and vision retrievers (DSE, ColPali, ColQwen, and multi-vector and dense Jina-embedding-v4), used text-only (visual elements via VLM descriptions), vision-only (page screenshots, no parsing) or hybrid. Sub-query results are reranked with Qwen3-reranker for text and accumulated equally per sub-query for vision and hybrid. Doc-Researcher runs with Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-235B or DeepSeek-R1 as backbone at three parsing levels: parsing-free (screenshots, plus InternVL3.5-38B to read them), shallow (fixed-length OCR chunks) and deep (layout-aware chunks with VLM transcriptions). Baselines are direct answering with no documents, long context (documents truncated at 96k tokens), and existing document RAG systems. The rest of the block is the text layer of Table 3, accuracy by language and domain, document-selection scores and retrieval recall per configuration; it is cut off inside the table.

Section 5.3, retrieval results (Table 2, details in Figure 7). Among text retrievers BM25 is weakest and dense retrievers (BGE-M3, Qwen3-Embedding) much better. Among vision retrievers Jina-embedding-v4, even dense, beats the other multi-vector models. Vision-only beats text-only on MMDocIR's visual tasks but not on M4DocBench's multi-document questions. Hybrid retrieval beats either single modality throughout: Qwen3-Embedding with Jina-embedding-v4 improves page recall by 8–12% over either alone. Sub-query decomposition helps every paradigm, for example Qwen3-Embedding page recall at k=15 from 42.1% to 49.9%. Recall falls with granularity: over 70% at document level for hybrid methods, 30–40 points lower at page and layout level.

Section 5.4, main results (Table 3). Direct answering scores 5–10% and long context 9–31%, while Doc-Researcher reaches 50.6%, which the authors take to show that research-level questions need a multi-agent workflow, not more context. Shallow parsing gives 34–39%, below parsing-free screenshots at 36–43%; deep parsing with hybrid retrieval gives 42–50%, about 10 points better. Baseline document RAG systems do poorly because they retrieve once with a fixed strategy: MDocAgent 15.8%, M3DocRAG 7.0%, ColQwen-gen 5.7%; Doc-Researcher's 50.6% is 3.4× MDocAgent. The block also holds the text layer and caption of Figure 3, accuracy, accumulated chunks and document, page and layout recall over search turns 1–5 for the three backbones, with accuracy gains of +7.2%, +9.7% and +11.1%.

Section 5.5, ablations. Within deep parsing, hybrid retrieval (42.4–50.6%) beats text-only (39.2–45.6%) by 3–5 points, so some visual meaning is lost even with good transcriptions. Removing the Planner costs 6–8 points, since the system then retrieves chunks uniformly from the noisy document set without filtering documents or choosing granularity. Over search turns (Figure 3), document recall rises from 62–65% at turn 1 to 75–82% at turn 3 and levels off near 82–83% by turn 5; accuracy rises from turn 1 to turn 5 by 7.2 points for Qwen3-32B, 9.7 for Qwen3-235B and 11.1 for DeepSeek-R1, mostly in turns 1–3, while accumulated chunks grow from 7–10 to 14–17. Stronger models use fewer chunks (DeepSeek-R1 14.1 against Qwen3-32B 17.2 at turn 5). Layout recall goes from 24–26% to 40–45%. The authors suggest three iterations as a good balance of quality and cost.

Section 5.6, efficiency (Table 4, whose text layer is in this block), on M4DocBench's 304 documents (6,177 pages, 4,146 figures, 2,739 tables) and 158 questions. Deep parsing takes about 2.5 hours up front, against 9–39 minutes for parsing-free indexing, mostly for MinerU layout analysis and VLM transcription. But at research time parsing-free methods spend about 20 hours, 80% of inference, reading screenshots, while deep parsing finishes the same questions in about 4 hours, a 5× speedup. Multi-vector embeddings take 10–20× the storage and about 4× the indexing time of dense ones, and current vector databases do not support their late-interaction search. For deep parsing, research time splits into about 2 hours planning, 4 hours of search-refine loops and 2 hours answering.

Conclusion. The authors restate their three contributions: deep multimodal parsing that keeps layout and modality-specific features (11.4% better than simple OCR), a retrieval architecture over text, vision and hybrid paradigms and chunk, page, full and summary granularities, and iterative multi-agent workflows with planning and search-refine loops (3.4× the best baseline); plus M4DocBench, 158 expert-annotated questions over 4 domains. Future work: compact multimodal embeddings, better cross-modal reasoning, and active learning that adapts retrieval to user interaction.

Reference list of the paper, pages 9–13: 46 numbered entries, 36 of them from 2024 or 2025 and 31 on arXiv. They cover vision-language models and embeddings (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3, BGE-M3, E5, ColPali, Jina-embedding-v4, DSE), document parsing (MinerU, UniMERNet), document VQA and RAG benchmarks and systems (MMDocIR, ViDoRe, DocBench, M3DocRAG, MDocAgent), and agentic RAG and deep-research systems.

Title and author block: "Doc-Researcher: A Unified System for Multimodal Document Parsing and Deep Research", by Kuicai Dong, Shurui Huang, Fangda Ye (co-first authors) and nine others at Huawei Technologies, with corresponding addresses for Dong and Yong Liu.
